prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which thousands of atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of first-order light shift and motional broadening, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock first, and I have not changed my configuration: B022 alone, Katori and Ye. What the round has done is sharpen the citation. The picture is the same as before: an egg-carton of light, tuned so that the trap shifts the two clock levels by the same amount, holds thousands of atoms still enough that Doppler and recoil effects disappear, and so statistics and systematics improve together. That is a specific idea, not clocks in general, and it is what separates it from the 2005 comb (a way to count optical cycles) and the 2012 prize (control of a single ion or photon). The claim that matters most to me as a theorist is that it was not obviously possible: the magic wavelength depends on the dynamic polarisabilities of two levels, and one must believe that higher-order multipole and hyperpolarisability shifts can be controlled at the 1e-18 level. Katori proposed the idea and made the first strontium demonstration; Ye's group showed that it works at the accuracy and stability frontier and compared clocks at that level. Independent laboratories now agree at that level and compare directly over fibre, which is the reproducibility I weigh most. Five of eight members now name this same two-name configuration, and I treat that as a consequence of the arguments, not as a reason.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is still that a committee could read this as a better instrument in a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and Danielsson's and Mehlig's point that so far the clock yields limits on drifting constants and dark matter, not detections, is fair. I answer that the new regime (many-atom interrogation, many-body effects, millimetre-scale redshift) is itself a physics result, but I accept that this is judgement. The credit is not airtight either: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and others are outside the two names, and I would not call it as clean as Kroll and Johansson do. I am confident about Katori's priority on the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstration and Ye's on performance and comparison, but I recall the early strontium papers from memory and the committee's experts should confirm the dates. The redefinition of the second has not happened, but I do not think recognition has to wait for it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B045 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) but says B022 is his first alternative and he would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested three-name list.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I agree that the quality of the Z2 idea and its HgTe confirmation is high; I defer to you on band topology. Your own case_against is the decisive part for me: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe experiment possible, Hasan led the 3D observation, and three names cannot honour that without looking arbitrary. The clock has no equivalent cut inside the two names. I do not claim B022 is free of overlap; the difference is that its overlap is with earlier prizes, not an unresolved split of credit among living contributors. If documentation settles the topological credit, I would reconsider B045, which is why I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig calls the lattice clock an application of known atomic physics (magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement) and places the conceptual novelty of a classifying invariant above a smaller uncertainty budget.
responses.response: This is the point I most want to answer, because as an atomic theorist I know exactly how much of the ingredients was known. Lamb-Dicke confinement and light shifts were known; what was not known was that one can choose a wavelength where the differential light shift of a narrow intercombination line vanishes while keeping the atoms in a deep lattice, and that the residual shifts (hyperpolarisability, multipole, tunnelling) can be pushed below 1e-18. The result is a new regime of quantum control over many atoms, not a smaller error bar, and a universal invariant is a different kind of achievement, not a bigger one. I think we weigh different things and I do not claim your criterion is wrong. You have said B022 is the safer prize if clean allocation weighs more, and I think it does.

responses.point: Kroll says Takamoto's 2005 demonstration is largely covered by Katori's name and that the Wineland overlap argument against B033 applies equally to B022, so it cannot be used against only one.
responses.response: I accept your last point; the overlap with Wineland applies to both and I will not use it selectively. I also agree that Takamoto's 2005 work belongs to Katori's group, but I disagree on Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley, whose strontium lattice work was independent and decisive for the accuracy frontier. That is why I would write the citation around the concept and the realisation, not around who reached the lowest number first, and why I think the committee should ask the experts for the dated record before the vote. On B033 versus B047, I ranked trapped ions low only because the proposal and demonstrations are split; I do not doubt the measured fidelities.

responses.point: Danielsson holds BAO first as a clean discovery and says he would not block B022, while asking whether a clock tells us something from nature or only improves a limit.
responses.response: I respect the BAO case, and the acoustic scale is exactly the kind of simple physics I like. I cannot judge the cosmology beyond that, and I still find a three-name BAO prize arbitrary when two survey collaborations made the detection and Peebles and Yu and Sunyaev and Zeldovich predicted the feature; the Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock trio cannot be called the unit. On your criterion, I would say the clock has already delivered a clue: the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the observation that atoms in a lattice interact collectively at this precision are things nature showed us once we could look. Limits on constants are so far limits, I agree, and I would not rest the case on them.

responses.point: Olsson regards the lattice clock as a discovery-and-invention case with Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength concept and Ye's 1e-18 performance, and also asks for checks on Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Lemonde.
responses.response: We agree on both the case and the open question. To the chair's question on the two-name unit, I would take it as: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for performance and the comparison between clocks. To the question of whether the lattice is a distinct invention from the comb and the ion clock, I would say the citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime, and I support your wording around interrogating large ensembles. Where I would adjust it slightly is to say invention and realisation, not invention and development, since Ye's contribution is performance, which is a part of realisation. I think that wording also gives the committee the best answer to the overlap with 2005 and 2012.

uncertainties: Priority and credit beyond Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and others), which I recall from memory only and which expert documentation should confirm, especially the dates of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock.

Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, which depends on the citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and not clocks in general.
Whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second; I think not, but I accept it as a legitimate view.
If B022 is set aside, whether the topological credit (Mele, Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) can be resolved in three names, and how to divide credit in B047 among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Cirac.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I have co-authored with Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato; I know of no connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock community, so I see no conflict for B022. For B047 I note that it is close to my own atomic physics field, though I have no personal tie to Bloch, Greiner, Zoller or Cirac. For B045 I have no tie to any credited name. Nothing has changed since round 1.
